transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Giles Snyder.
President Trump is offering $1 million for evidence of voter fraud in past elections
and in the upcoming midterms.
The bounty is reminiscent of ones offered by Trump supporters after the 2020 election.
However, voter fraud happens, it's far too rare to swing national elections.
Trump's reward for information that leads to a conviction comes as Democrats prepare
for Trump to allege election fraud in the midterms.
NPR's Eric McDaniel reports that Trump has alleged fraudulent behavior in every election
he's been involved with since 2016.
Here's Congressman Joe Morelli, Democrat of New York, on a recent call with reporters.
We have seen a nationwide effort of lawmakers, litigators, organizers and activists, some
of the brightest minds in the nation working with one goal in mind.
The successful administration of free and fair elections in 2026.
In particular, Democratic lawmakers are concerned that the president will declare foreign interference
or wrongly claim victory in key races.
The White House has repeatedly told NPR that the president is working to ensure American
elections are secure.
The president told a reporter earlier this month that he would honor the results of the
midterm elections.
He's also taken preemptive steps in one state to challenge the outcome if the Republican
candidate doesn't win, Eric McDaniel and PR News in Washington.
The Justice Department has charged former FBI Director James Comey with mishandling national
security information.
NPR's Kerry Johnson reports on the third time the Trump administration has brought criminal
charges against Comey.
Prosecutors in Washington, D.C. charged the prominent critic of President Trump using
a criminal complaint.
That means they still must persuade a grand jury to indict James Comey, a step that's
not a foregone conclusion in D.C.
The former head of the FBI says he's innocent and will fight the new case.
The charges come the same day a judge found DOJ unlawfully fired Comey's daughter, Maureen.
The administration never gave any performance-related explanation for firing her from her job as
a federal prosecutor in New York.
Kerry Johnson, NPR News.
The A.I. giant, anthropic, has filed paperwork for an initial public offering.
They say it could be one of the biggest on record, as NPR's Sean Ruich reports.
Anthropic got its start just five years ago when a group of senior researchers at Open
A.I. led by Dario Amadeh broke away.
They were concerned that the company was not on a path to develop A.I. safely.
Anthropic has since become a juggernaut and Open A.I.'s biggest competitor was some of
the most widely used A.I. models on the market.
Amadeh, now CEO, has issued some of the A.I. world's sharpest warnings about the possibility
of A.I. spiraling out of human control.
The IPO prospectus showed skyrocketing growth at the company, and analysts say the IPO could
value the firm at $1.5 to $2 trillion.
John Ruich, NPR News.
And you're listening to NPR News.
A court hearing is set for tomorrow afternoon, in a case involving some 20,000 people on
California's voter rolls.
The Justice Department wants any ballots from them set aside, alleging they should not be
counted because they belong to non-citizen voters.
In a 2-1 decision Monday night, an appeals court dismissed a DOJ appeal in the case,
setting up Tuesday's hearing before a federal district judge.
California officials say that list is unreliable and that it is not feasible to set aside the
ballots this close to Election Day.
Director Walter Koenig, an original cast member of the television series Star Trek, has died
as agents as he was 90 years old, and that he died at his home in Los Angeles, and Piers
Mendele Del Barco reports.
On Star Trek, Walter Koenig played Pavel Chekov, a baby-faced ensign from Russia who navigated
the Starship Enterprise.
Chekov was always boasting about Russian inventions, and with a wig like Davy Jones from The Monkees,
he appealed to the younger generation.
Here he is on NPR in 1976, talking about Chekov.
I'll give you one of my deathless lines that I'm sure long after I have expired and my
ashes have blown in the wind, I will be known for.
Warp tiktar vor kibtin.
Ensign Chekov would go on to become a Starfleet officer in Star Trek movies, and Walter Koenig
acted in another sci-fi TV show, Babylon 5.
He wrote several TV episodes, and also two memoirs, Mandelit Del Barco, NPR News.
And I'm Giles Snyder.
This is NPR.
This message comes from Rosetta Stone, offering an alternative approach to language learning.

in a second language.
More information at RosettaStone.com.

topics.text: Trump offers $1 million bounty for evidence of voter fraud in past and upcoming elections
Trump has alleged fraudulent behavior in every election since 2016, NPR reports
Justice Department charges former FBI Director James Comey with mishandling national security information
Judge rules DOJ unlawfully fired Comey's daughter Maureen, a federal prosecutor in New York
Anthropic files paperwork for initial public offering, possibly valued at $1.5 to $2 trillion
Court hearing set for Tuesday over Justice Department bid to set aside California ballots of 20,000 voters
Star Trek actor Walter Koenig, who played Chekov, dies at 90 in Los Angeles
